chunks: Replace the brushes or the motor?. The question: When should you replace brushes vs replace the whole motor?
When a brushed motor stops working because its brushes are worn, you must decide whether to replace the brushes or the whole motor.
It depends on whether the brushes can be replaced at all, what condition the rest of the motor is in, and what each option costs.
Also ask why the brushes wore out, or the new ones will fail the same way.
It is like a worn tire on a car. If the rest of the car is healthy, you replace the tires. If the engine and frame are also worn out, you buy a different car.
A sealed toy motor is more like a disposable item, where the "tire" cannot be changed at all.
The analogy has a gap: with a motor you must inspect the commutator and bearings to know how healthy the rest is.
Decision flow. Serviceability and commutator condition come first; windings and bearings next; economics last.
"Fix the root cause" applies on every path where the brush failure was premature.
Serviceable: designed so you can open it and change the brushes. Brush kit: a set of replacement brushes and springs. Commutator: the copper segments the brushes slide on.
It should be round and evenly colored. Bearings: the parts the shaft turns in. They should have no play (looseness) or noise.
Root cause: the real reason the part failed, such as overload or arcing.
Take a power drill with worn brushes. Its brush holders are easy to reach. The commutator is smooth with an even brown film, and the bearings are quiet.
So you replace the brushes and the drill is nearly like new. Now take a small sealed toy motor with worn brushes.
The brushes are part of the can and cannot be changed, so you replace the motor.
That is the whole idea: replace the brushes if they are accessible and the rest is healthy, otherwise replace the motor.
"It depends on serviceability, condition and cost.
If the motor has accessible brush holders and a standard kit, and the commutator is round with a good film, the bearings and windings are fine, then replacing the worn brushes restores it cheaply.
If the commutator is grooved, burnt or below minimum size, or windings or bearings are failing, or the motor is a sealed consumable, replace the motor.
Compare repair cost over the extra life with the new-motor cost, and fix the cause of the wear."
